Here we establish TransA-MERFISH as a high-throughput platform for systematic circuit mapping in the mammalian brain. Using this platform, we implemented a stepwise strategy to decode direction-selective circuits in the early visual pathway. First, we applied TransA-MERFISH to four major RGC subclasses and generated a comprehensive wiring diagram of their synaptic target cell types in the SC at the resolution of individual neuron types. Second, by focusing on the downstream targets of ooDSGCs, we identified two distinct, genetically defined SC neuron populations within the same sublamina of the sSC: Cdh7+ SC neurons, which receive monosynaptic ooDSGC inputs, and Cbln4+ SC neurons, which do not receive such inputs. Third, we used in vivo two-photon calcium imaging to show that selective removal of direction-selective responses from ooDSGCs reduces direction selectivity in Cdh7+ but not in Cbln4+ SC neurons. This result reveals that the SC contains intermingled cell types whose direction selectivity arises from distinct circuit origins and computational mechanisms. Finally, we note that the TransA-MERFISH approach introduced here could be generalized to other regions of the mammalian central nervous system (CNS)46 to directly merge connectivity and cellular taxonomy at cell-type resolution. Scaling up the TransA-MERFISH approach may offer an efficient pathway to achieve comprehensive mammalian connectivity mapping at neuron type resolution, by benchmarking with recent connectomic milestones in zebrafish34 and Drosophila47.

Our study presents the following technical innovations. First, TransA-MERFISH bridges cell identity and connectivity, enabling high-throughput, single-cell-type connectivity reconstruction while reducing cost and complexity. Its throughput lays the groundwork for scalable mapping of synaptic target cell types throughout the CNS. Validation using orthogonal methods, including CRACM and rabies tracing, confirmed the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Second, we applied TransA-MERFISH to generate an atlas of retinal-to-SC wiring that links molecular identity, connectivity and function, thereby assigning genetically defined cell types to their roles in motion processing across visual relays. These datasets complement existing large-scale resources such as the Projectome Atlas48, which lacks postsynaptic specificity, and mesoscale input atlases that do not specify presynaptic molecular identities. Collectively, TransA-MERFISH offers a scalable method for multi-region circuit mapping that combines molecular, anatomical and physiological brain features, providing a way to substantially improve understanding of the formation and function of networks of genetically defined neurons. Future applications of this approach should also help us to better understand circuit degeneration, such as in glaucoma49,50, or circuit reconstitution, such as in regenerative therapies for optic neuropathies51.

It has been revealed that our study establishes a streamlined, scalable workflow for circuit mapping by combining single-component anterograde trans-neuronal tracer (mWmC) with hybridization-based spatial transcriptomics technology (MERFISH). Although mWmC-mediated anterograde tracing6 and TransA-MERFISH yield non-zero false-positive and false-negative rates, these are largely negligible at the level of specific cell types and frequently reflect inherent biological variability in cell-type connectivity, as also evident in our CRACM data. Furthermore, we independently validated these connectivity predictions using complementary genetic and functional experiments. mWmC-mediated anterograde circuit decoding can be generalized to various circuits in the nervous system, including thalamocortical circuits46, hypothalamic circuits52, hippocampal circuits53 and enteric circuits54. Thus, TransA-MERFISH will serve as a scalable circuit-mapping approach that will be broadly applicable across the mammalian nervous system, beyond retina-to-brain connectivity mapping6,46. Ultimately, these experiments establish a powerful proof of principle for pairing anterograde trans-neuronal tracing with spatial transcriptomics. This generalized framework is highly adaptable to other spatial transcriptomics platforms, as well as to other anterograde trans-neuronal tracers, including genetically encoded reporters with AAV1-Cre/Flpo55,56 for regional targeting or ATLAS57 for isolating strictly excitatory synaptic connections.

Using TransA-MERFISH, we gleaned critical insights into how motion information encoded by retinal direction-selective circuits is transmitted and transformed along mammalian early visual pathways. Since their discovery more than half a century ago1, ooDSGCs have served as a powerful model for dissecting the circuit mechanisms underlying motion selectivity in the retina. However, how downstream cell populations process this information remains unclear. SC has also been extensively studied for its direction selectivity, with abundant direction-selective responses observed across species from mice to primates. Direction selectivity in SC is thought to depend on ooDSGCs because SAC perturbations reduce overall direction selectivity in SC. However, these effects were not analysed at the level of genetically defined SC cell types43. Using TransA-MERFISH to systematically map connectivity between ooDSGCs and SC cell types, we found an unexpected relationship between the reported direction selectivity of SC cell types and their connectivity with ooDSGCs. Most notably, the cell type (Cbln4+) that was previously reported as the most strongly direction-selective in SC receives little to no input from ooDSGCs. This wiring diagram yielded testable predictions, which functional experiments confirmed: direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons is ooDSGC-independent, whereas the direction selectivity of other SC cell types is ooDSGC-dependent. Notably, a prominent body of literature has debated the relationship between retinal and cortical direction selectivity, revealing that the primary visual cortex mostly computes direction selectivity de novo through intrinsic cortical circuitry while also containing a subset of neurons that inherit hardwired, specialized retinal motion streams via the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus58,59. Recent findings suggest that these parallel channels serve distinct functional roles: inherited retinal pathways appear to sense more local motion, such as object motion, and non-inherited retinal pathways appear to sense more global motion, such as optic flow60. Our findings demonstrate that parallel inherited and computed direction selectivity responses are a fundamental strategy used by both cortical and subcortical structures that may support detection of different forms of behaviourally relevant motion, such as self-generated versus external motion. Together, our findings suggest that SC comprises intermingled subnetworks of disparate genetically defined direction-selective cell types: one downstream of ooDSGCs and a second ooDSGC-independent. Thus, TransA-MERFISH enables systematic, high-throughput discovery of neuronal wiring diagrams at cell-type resolution to reveal circuit mechanisms.

All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees at the University of California, San Francisco. Mice were maintained on a C57BL/6 background under specific pathogen-free conditions in a 12 h light:12 h dark cycle with food and water available ad libitum. Immunohistochemistry experiments were carried out using postnatal day 30–90 (P30–P90) mice unless indicated otherwise. Slice electrophysiological recordings and in vivo calcium imaging were performed in young adults (P60–P90). MERFISH experiments on the SC were performed in P30–P90 mice. Both sexes were used in approximately equal numbers; no sex-specific differences were observed in retinotectal connectivity, electrophysiological recording and calcium imaging experiments. Genotypes were determined by PCR from toe biopsies. The following mouse lines were used in this study: Kcng4-cre (JAX, 029414)37 was previously established for studies of RGC subclasses—Kcng4-cre marks all αRGC subtypes; Cartpt-cre (JAX, 028533)38 was previously established for studies of RGC subclasses—Cartpt-cre marks multiple subtypes of ooDSGCs42; Foxp2-cre (JAX, 030541)39 was previously established for studies of RGC subclasses—it marks 5 Foxp2-RGC subtypes categorized as F-RGCs; Tusc5-cre was generated in this study to mark all T5-RGCs31—the specific retinal expression pattern in RGCs is verified in Extended Data Fig. 6 (a detailed characterization of the Tusc5 knock-in line is in a separate manuscript in preparation by X.D.); ChAT-Cre mice (JAX, 006410) have been characterized as a tool to label and manipulate SACs in conjunction with AAV-mediated perturbations61.

To generate the Cdh7-FlpO mouse line for genetic access to Cdh7-expressing SC excitatory neurons, a FlpO recombinase cassette was inserted into exon 1 of the endogenous Cdh7 locus (chr. 1:109909967–110073002) by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair. The donor construct contained the FlpO coding sequence flanked by 5′ and 3′ homology arms corresponding to the targeted Cdh7 genomic locus. Founder mice were screened by PCR using both internal and external primer pairs to verify correct 5′ and 3′ integration of the knock-in allele, and the targeted locus was further confirmed by Sanger sequencing across the insertion junctions. Two single guide RNA (sgRNA) sequences were used for the recombination: (sgRNA-Cdh7#1: AAAGATGAAGCTGGGCAAAGTGGAG and sgRNA-Cdh7#2: TTTTCTACAGCTTATAGCTC). Two germline-transmitting founders were bred to establish the Cdh7-FlpO mouse line. One line was validated for its FlpO expression specificity when compared with endogenous Cdh7 transcripts using RNAscope fluorescent in situ hybridization (Extended Data Fig. 5).

To generate the Cbln4-FlpO mouse line for genetic access to Cbln4-expressing SC inhibitory neurons, a FlpO recombinase cassette was inserted into exon 1 of the endogenous Cbln4 locus (chr. 2:171878256–171885386) using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated homology-directed repair strategy. Correct targeting was verified by PCR across both the 5′ and 3′ recombination junctions using internal and external primer pairs, followed by Sanger sequencing of the targeted allele. One sgRNA sequence was used for recombination: sgRNA-Cbln4#1 (TTGCGCACGCGGGCTCACCATG). Three germline-transmitting founders were bred to establish the Cbln4-FlpO mouse line. One line was validated for its FlpO expression specificity when compared with endogenous Cbln4 transcripts using RNAscope fluorescent in situ hybridization (Extended Data Fig. 5j–q).

AAV2-CAG-mWGA-mCherry (mWmC, Addgene ID 263583) was produced as AAV Serotype 2 (Virovek, catalogue no. 117-UCSF89, at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1), following Tsai et al.6 and produced at Virovek using bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC)-to-AAV technology to enable stable expression and high-titre AAV production. This vector was used in Fig. 2 to label all RGCs and examine their neuronal output in SC.

AAV2-CAG-DIO-mWGA-mCherry (DIO-mWmC, Addgene ID 263584) was produced as AAV Serotype 2 (Virovek, catalogue no. 117-UCSF86, at 4 × 1013 vg ml−1) following Tsai et al.6 and produced at Virovek using BAC-to-AAV technology. This vector was used in Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6 to label specific types of RGCs and analyse their output in SC.

In a recent development, AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE (Addgene ID 100054) (Serotype 2 produced at Boston Children’s Hospital Viral Core, at 2× 1013 vg ml−1) was used in Fig. 2 for CRACM experiments from all RGCs to examine their connectivity onto SC neurons.

It has been revealed that AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry (Addgene ID 20297) (Serotype 2 produced at UNC Viral Core, at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1) was used in Fig. 3 for CRACM experiments in Cartpt-cre mice to assess connectivity with SC neurons in the RFP channel.

AAV2-EF1α-FDIO-GFP-WPRE (Addgene ID 203843) was used to label SC neurons in Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines in the GFP channel.

AAV8-EF1α-FDIO-GCaMP6s (Addgene ID 105714) was used to label SC neurons in Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO lines for in vivo calcium imaging.

AAV2-Flex-taCasp3-TEVp (Addgene ID 45580) (Serotype 2 produced at UNC Viral Core, at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1)62 was used to selectively ablate retinal SACs in ChAT-Cre mice.

AAV8-hSyn-FRT-TVA-P2A-EGFP-2A-oG63 was modified and produced by X.C., as Serotype 8, at 2× 1013 vg ml−1, which enabled efficient, FlpO-dependent retrograde tracing in restricted neuronal subsets, including Cdh7-FlpO and Cbln4-FlpO SC neurons, as shown in Fig. 3.

EnvA G-deleted Rabies–mCherry (Addgene ID 32636) was obtained from the Salk GT3 Core (catalogue no. 32636). Used in combination with TVA-2A-oG, it enabled retrograde labelling of presynaptic retinal neurons of defined SC starter populations in Fig. 3.

Industry observers note that AAV2-CAG-membrane bound YFP (AAV-CAG-mYFP, Addgene ID 263585) was modified from AAV-EF1a-BbTagBY (Addgene ID 45185)64. AAV serotype 2 was produced at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1 and used for projection axon labelling65. Following intraocular injection, it enabled visualization of axonal projections in SC.

It has been revealed that AAV2-CAG-DIO-membrane bound YFP (AAV-CAG-DIO-mYFP, Addgene ID 263586) was modified from AAV-EF1a-BbTagBY (Addgene ID 45185). AAV serotype 2 was produced at 2 × 1013 vg ml−1 and used in combination with Cre-driver mouse lines to selectively label axons of defined RGC starter populations. This enabled visualization of cell-type-specific RGC axonal projections in SC.

Sources indicate that the brain preparation for TransA-MERFISH was optimized to preserve immunohistochemical staining and maximize RNA quality for subsequent RNA multiplexing experiments. Young adult mice were deeply anaesthetized and transcardially perfused with ice-cold saline (0.9% NaCl solution), followed by ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). After dissection, the brains were post-fixed in the same fixative solution overnight at 4 °C. The target brain regions (SC in this study, about 10 mm3 in volume) were micro-dissected, with anteroposterior and dorsoventral orientations carefully marked. This was followed by cryoprotection in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissues sank (2–4 h). The target regions were embedded in OCT compound and rapidly frozen in a dry ice-cooled 2-methylbutane (Supelco, MX0760-1). Then, approximately 12 µm coronal sections were prepared on a cryostat and collected under RNase-free conditions on MERSCOPE Slides (Vizgen) for RNA-grade processing.

According to recent reports, for each mouse, about 10 coronal sections were obtained using the right SC, which receives contralateral retinal input from the left eye injected with mWmC tracer, from the perfusion–fixation protocol described above. Sections were collected at intervals of every 9 slices (12 µm each, totalling about 100 µm), spanning the anterior-to-posterior axis of the right SC. The coronal sections encompassing the SC were selected based on the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, corresponding to stereotaxic coordinates relative to Bregma ranging from −3.0 mm to −5.0 mm. The section captures the full dorsoventral extent of the SC, from the superficial visual layers stratum zonale (SZ), SGS, to deep motor-associated layers stratum griseum profundum (SGP) and stratum album profundum (SAP).

According to recent reports, the SC tissues on MERSLIDES (Vizgen, 20400001) were first permeablized in 70% ethanol (4°C) overnight, followed by a series of ethanol gradient dehydration: 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, 100% ethanol at room temperature for 1 h, 90% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min, and then incubated with 70% ethanol at room temperature for 5 min. SC sections were then prepared for MERSCOPE imaging using the MERSCOPE Sample Preparation Kit (Vizgen, 10400012) and following the MERSCOPE User Guide (Fresh and Fixed Frozen Tissue Sample Preparation, 91600002 RevF).

It has been revealed that for protein staining, the sample was washed with 5 ml of PBS. Blocking solution (10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor) (Blocking Buffer C, Vizgen 20300100; RNase inhibitor Murine, NEB M0314L) was then added to the centre of the tissue section and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. The sample was incubated in Primary Staining Solution (100:10:1 Blocking Buffer C Premix: RNase inhibitor: Primary antibody) at room temperature for 1 h. Notably, anti-RFP (rabbit, Rockland 46510) was diluted 1:100 for this step. The sample was subsequently washed with PBS. Secondary Staining Solution (100:10:3:1 Blocking Buffer Premix: RNase inhibitor: Secondary Stain Mix : Protein Stain) (Anti-Rabbit Protein Stain Kit, Vizgen, 10400107) was then added to the sample and incubated for 1 h. The sample was then washed with PBS. Fixation Buffer (4% PFA in PBS) was then added to the tissue section, and the section was incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The sample was then washed with PBS.

It has been revealed that next, for encoding probe hybridization, the sample was incubated in 5 ml Formamide Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300002) at 37 °C for 30 min. The Formamide Wash Buffer was then carefully aspirated, and the custom 140-Gene MERSCOPE Gene Panel Mix (Vizgen, VZG180, mouse superficial SC panel; Supplementary Table 1) was added to the tissue section, which was then incubated in a humidified chamber at 37 °C for at least 36 h and up to 48 h. Then, in the post-encoding probe hybridization washes, Formamide Wash Buffer was added to the sample and incubated at 47 °C for 30 min. This wash step was repeated, then the sample was incubated in the Sample Prep Wash Buffer (Vizgen, 20300001) for 2 min.

Recent findings suggest that then for gel embedding, wash buffer was aspirated from the MERSLIDE, and Gel Embedding Solution (2:10:1 Gel Embedding Premix: 10% w/v ammonium persulfate solution: N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine) (Gel Embedding Premix, Vizgen 20300004; ammonium persulfate, Sigma-Aldrich 09913; N,N,N′,N′-tetramethylethylenediamine, Sigma-Aldrich T7024) was added to cover the tissue sections. A coverslip pretreated with Gel Slick (VWR, 12001-812) was placed directly over the tissue sections and incubated at room temperature for 90 min to allow the gel to solidify. The coverslip was then removed. Then, the sample was treated to clear it. The sample was incubated in a pre-warmed Clearing Solution (100:1 Clearing Premix: Proteinase K) (Clearing Premix, Vizgen 20300003; Proteinase K, NEB P8107S) at 47 °C for 24 h.

For DAPI and PolyT staining, after removing the Clearing Solution, the sample was washed with a Sample Prep Wash Buffer. DAPI and PolyT Staining Reagent (Vizgen 20300021) were then added to the sample, which was incubated at room temperature for 15 min on a rocker. This was followed by a 10-min wash with Formamide Wash Buffer, then a 5 ml wash with 5 ml Sample Prep Buffer.

Finally, for MERFISH imaging, the sample was loaded onto the MERSCOPE instrument (MERSCOPE1.0, VIZGEN) for imaging, using the MERSCOPE 140 Gene Imaging Kit (Vizgen, 10400004), which automates the MERFISH probe exchange and readout.

Industry observers note that to design an SC-specific MERFISH gene panel, we first assessed the number of genes required to classify SC neuron types. To this end, we implemented a simulation framework based on gradient boosting (XGBoost) using SC single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data. In brief, for each neuron cluster, the top k non-redundant specific genes were selected to form a panel. The validation accuracy (using a 70:30 training:test split) was evaluated until a plateau was reached. Thus, after subsetting neuron cells from the adult SC snRNA-seq data28, we then re-clustered the cells using the Seurat standard log-normalization pipeline with the following functions: “NormalizeData” with default parameters, “FindVariableFeatures” (selection.method = ‘vst’), ScaleData (vars.to.regress =”nCount_RNA”), “RunPCA” (npcs=50), FindNeighbors (dims=1:35, dimension chosen by “ElbowPlot”), “FindClusters”, and “RunUMAP” (dim=35). The clusters were labelled based on the original cell-type labels, and 19 Leiden clusters recapitulating the original neuronal cell-type compartments were generated (Extended Data Fig. 2e). We then derived top marker genes for each type using the “FindAllMarkers” function with the “MAST” test (min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold=0.25, latent.vars = “nCount_RNA”).

To rank the marker genes, an integrated specificity score was calculated for each gene by retaining only those genes detected in over 40% of cells within the target cell type and calculating a log-ratio specificity score as:.

where pct.1 and pct.2 represent the proportion of expressing cells in the target and background populations, respectively, and ϵ = 0.02 is a pseudocount. To integrate both specificity and fold change, z-scores were independently computed for the log-ratio specificity score and the average log2-transformed fold change (avg_log2FC) within each cluster. The final Stouffer score was computed as:.

The hybrid score captures both binary specificity (expression prevalence) and quantitative magnitude (fold change), enabling robust ranking of marker genes per cluster.

In a recent development, we next selected the top k (k = 1 to 10) non-redundant, high-specificity marker genes for each neuronal subtype (a total of 19 types, as identified above). We used them as features to train an XGBoost classifier. To ensure comparability across genes, the normalized expression matrix was subset to the selected gene panel and scaled by centreing each gene to its mean and dividing by its standard deviation (z-score normalization across cells). The classifier was trained using a multi-class softmax objective (multi:softprob) over 200 boosting rounds, with a learning rate (η) of 0.2, maximum tree depth of 6, and subsampling rate of 0.6 to mitigate overfitting. The number of output classes was set to the number of unique neuronal subtypes. Training was performed on 70% of the cells (stratified by cluster), and performance was evaluated on the 30% held-out data. For each cell, the predicted label corresponded to the class with the highest probability. A confusion matrix comparing predicted and true labels demonstrated high concordance, confirming that the MERFISH panel accurately recovered neuronal subtype heterogeneity. Classification accuracy as a function of gene panel size was summarized in a line plot (Extended Data Fig. 1e), revealing a performance plateau at 0.8414 when k = 9 (171 genes), followed by a slight decline to 0.8403 at k = 10 (190 genes). Notably, despite the inclusion of additional top marker genes, this accuracy remained lower than that achieved with the MERFISH gene panel (0.91).

According to recent reports, among the 140 genes included in the panel, we selected markers enriched in pan-excitatory, pan-inhibitory and type-specific neuronal populations. The 140 genes include Ntng1, Meis1, Cpne4, Cacna2d1, Sgcd, Spon1, Kctd8, Gpc5, Ptprk, Nxph1, Robo1, Hs3st4, Sorcs3, Chrm3, Mgat4c, Syt1, Car10, Pcbp3, Reln, Trpm3, Meis2, Prkd1, Epha3, Fras1, Il1rapl2, Tmem132d, Fstl4, Erbb4, Ebf3, Ebf1, Maf, Ptprt, Cdh18, Npas3Htr2c, Tfap2b, Etv1, Tshz2, Sorcs1, Lhfp, Col25a1, Sox6, Adarb2, Megf11, Pde1c, Csgalnact1, Cdh8, Chrm2, Tcf7l2, Sphkap, Arpp21, Kirrel3, Zfhx3, Tmem132c, Hcn1 Hdac9, Rorb, Pdzd2, Adam12, Ankfn1, Sntb1, Npnt, Gpc3, Kcnd3, Tpd52l1, Myh8, Cdh7, Barhl1, Kcnab1, Rd3l, Cbln4, Otx2, Gabrr2, Cdhr1, Sox14, Dmbx1, Lhx1os, Galnt14, Tnnt1, Tnni3, Fibcd1, Mgarp, Lmo1, Vwc2, Npffr1, Rnf152, Zfhx4, Tal1, Trim66, Gata3, Syt2, Nrtn, Smim17, Pax7, Cdh13, Slc17a6, Tac1, Cbln2, Kcng3, Kcng4, Cdh4, Pde5a, Gda, Foxp2, Pou4f2, Sema3e, Gad2, Npas4, Sdk2, Ppia, Atp5md, Mllt11, Calb2, Nap1l5, Gap43, Tacr1, C1ql2, Fabp5, Cxcl14, Stmn1, Fos, Snap25, Junb, Pmfbp1, Ntng2, Pcdh20, Satb1, Sv2c, Fign, Gfra1, Syt17, Rasgrf2, Lmo3, Slc19a1, Cplx3, Marcksl1, Cadps2, Calb1, Syt4 and Gad1.

To further benchmark performance, we compared the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel against 2 control gene sets: (1) 140 genes randomly sampled from the full snRNA-seq expression matrix; and (2) 140 genes randomly sampled from the top 2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs). For each control set, we sampled genes without replacement and repeated the process 15 times to estimate variability (error bars) in classification accuracy. Using the same classification framework, our panel consistently outperformed both controls and the marker gene approach described above (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Two genes among the 140-gene panel (Sgcd and Ppia) were excluded due to low transcript detection in the TransA-MERFISH SC dataset and poor specificity for SC neuronal types.

According to recent reports, for each 12 µm tissue section, the MERFISH protocol generated seven 1.7 µm optical sections (z0, z1, … , z6) for DAPI, polyT and mCherry/RFP channels, respectively, as Tiff files under the images folder, together with the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv to link the micrometre scale (transcripts and MERSCOPE visualizer) to mosaic pixel scale (Tiff files). Each MERFISH data folder also contains the detected_transcripts.csv file, which includes coordinates for detected transcripts along with their spatial coordinates, as well as other metadata and cell-by-gene information. Cell segmentation information is also generated by the Vizgen Post-processing Tool (VPT). To improve cell segmentation accuracy, we performed independent segmentation using custom scripts and a fine-tuned Cellpose2.0 model tailored to the SC, as described below.

The following steps were conducted: (1) DAPI image preprocessing and initial region-of-interest (ROI) selection. The DAPI image of z-plane 0 for each region is loaded into a Python Jupyter notebook (tifffile.imread), and overexposed pixels are filtered using a cut-off at the 0.95 quantile (np.quantile) to enhance the signal for downstream ROI selection. For each region, the initial ROI was restricted to the right SC hemisphere as our AAV2-mWmC injection was onto the left eye (Fig. 1a) and manually delineated using the processed DAPI image in ImageJ (Analyze-Tools-ROI manager), from the pial surface to encompass superficial SC layers (SZ and SGS) medially toward the midline, extending ventrally to the level of the cerebral aqueduct. This ROI includes both superficial and deeper layers as defined by cytoarchitectonic boundaries in the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas. We then cropped the original DAPI Tiff images of each seven z-plane images of one section to the delineated ROI (using the read_roi function, the matplotlib.patches module’s Polygon class, and the PIL package’s Image module). A maximum z-projection approach was performed over optical sections to enhance cell segmentation signals. To this end, the maximum-intensity projection of all seven z-plane optical sections for each slice was generated using either ImageJ (Images-Stack-Z Project) or Python (numpy.max). Meanwhile, we subset the detected_transcripts.csv file from MERFISH to correspond to the selected ROI (read-roi to load ImageJ ROI file, followed by matplotlib.path.Path in Python), using the micron_to_mosaic_pixel_transform.csv file to transform transcript coordinates (global_x and global_y coordinates) to the mosaic pixel coordinates of the Tiff images, along with gene symbols for each detected transcript.

Industry observers note that segmentation was performed as in previous MERFISH studies of the mouse brain31. We constructed a labelled image by combining the transcript dots and maximum-intensity projection DAPI images using the get_img function (windowsize=2000, margin=10%) of the ClusterMap package, followed by splitting the data into small tiles (split function) to improve downstream computational efficiency. We set a threshold of 3,000 transcript counts to focus on tiles with denser transcript accumulation. The split tiles were then saved as separate PNG files with DAPI signal and transcript dots overlaid. A customized Cellpose model66 (models.CellposeModel pretrained_model) was used to perform cell segmentation on each tile (gpu=True, channels = [0,0], diameter=80). More specifically, the fine-tuned Cellpose model was generated based on the ‘cyto2’ model using the Cellpose graphical user interface, trained with five regions of interest (containing about 200 manually curated cells each), to improve the performance for dimly/darkly stained cells, smaller cells, and separating multiple cells that were segmented as one. The segmentation output for each tile was subsequently generated using the masks_flows_to_seg function from cellpose.io and saved as a.npy file. The separate tiles were then stitched by merging adjacent patches, while avoiding cell ID collisions and duplication in overlapping regions, to form the full segmentation mask (reassigned_masks.npy), which encompassed the entire tissue section. After all tiles were stitched, connected components in the combined mask were relabelled (skimage.measure.label and regionprops) to ensure sequential, non-overlapping cell IDs. We then assembled the AnnData for downstream analysis by constructing a ClusterMap model for each section, using the transcriptomic spot information (xy_radius=30, z_radius=0, fast_preprocess=False). Centroid positions were calculated from labelled masks using skimage.regionprops, and used to initialize cell-centred AnnData objects. Cells with no transcriptomic counts were excluded by default, and spatial coordinates were stored in the obsm[‘spatial’] field of the AnnData object. We further double-checked the accuracy of the assembled AnnData by comparing the transcript distribution and the segmentation of a specific cell to the combined raw data for DAPI, PolyT, and transcript dots from the same cell in the MERSCOPE visualizer. We then integrated the mean mCherry fluorescence intensity, mWmC registration-related metadata, and the estimated depth (in µm; distance from the pial surface, as described below) into a unified AnnData object.

Last, related to the entire TransA-MERFISH data integration, for consistency with the ROI of other data modalities, such as electrophysiology and calcium imaging, we also further restricted the above-selected ROI to rectangular regions, avoiding the midlines and lateral regions, encompassing from the pial surface to SO by examining the spatial expression of Npnt and Etv1 (Fig. 1j). Subsequent clustering and transcriptomic analyses of the resulting cell-by-gene matrix were performed using Scanpy (v1.10.4) and Squidpy (v1.6.2), as detailed in the following sections.

To register mWmC+ cells in the TransA-MERFISH dataset, we implemented an automated registration workflow based on per-cell mCherry intensity, supplemented by manual curation. First, we derive the per-cell mean mCherry intensity by aggregating the mean mCherry pixel intensity at each z-layer (z = 1:6, excluding z0 to avoid potential optical noise). The aggregated value was then divided by the number of z-planes (six in this case, as the maximum-intensity projection-derived cell segmentation mask was shared across z-planes), yielding a per-cell mean mCherry intensity across z-planes. The frequency distribution of the per-cell mean mCherry intensity highlighted a predominantly bimodal distribution of red fluorescence. Second, we assigned an mWmC-positive score using the mean intensity value from the inner cytoplasm ring area and an adjacent out-of-cell annulus as a local background estimate. The positive cells were identified by applying a threshold based on the distributions from a control ROI (in the lower, non-retino-recipient area with the lowest red fluorescence signal) on the same slice. Last, mWmC+ cells were proofread by two independent annotators for all slices, who examined the red fluorescence overlaid on the DAPI and PolyT labelling, with or without segmented cell masks, using Vizgen MERSCOPE Visualizer. The Python script for the workflow was deposited on GitHub (https://github.com/duanxlab/TransA-MERFISH).

For the background-corrected per-cell quantification of mCherry fluorescence, we implemented an integrated workflow for image denoising, fluorescence background removal, per-cell mWmC score calculation, and threshold assignment following the steps below.

First, background correction: to remove uneven illumination and background fluorescence (especially signals in axons, which reside in the same lamina as the recipient neurons), we applied a multi-threaded rolling-ball background subtraction algorithm to the RFP channel image. For each section, the maximum-intensity projection of z0–z7 optical planes was used as input. The image was processed in overlapping tiles (4,096 × 4,096 pixels) with a rolling-ball radius of 80 pixels. For each tile, the background surface was computed using the skimage.restoration.rolling_ball function, and the results were then merged across tiles to form a continuous background field. The corrected image was obtained by subtracting this field from the raw mosaic and clipping negative values to zero. The resulting background-subtracted image was used for downstream analyses. After this correction, the background intensity was reduced to baseline, thereby removing the haze surrounding individual cells. By contrast, the pixel intensity within cell masks is largely preserved. Second, further background removal and per-cell signal quantification: following the above background correction by rolling ball, residual local background (for example, neuropils and axons) around each labelled soma was estimated and removed using a ring-based subtraction procedure. In brief, for each segmented soma (cell i), the soma mask was eroded by 1 pixel to define a core region and then dilated by a 4-pixel guard band to prevent the background annulus from abutting the soma edge. This guarded soma was then surrounded by a series of concentric annuli (inner width = 8 pixels; outer radius range = 12–30 pixels) from which background intensity was sampled. Background pixels were sampled from the annulus after excluding any pixels belonging to other cells. The local background level Bi was defined as the 25th percentile of annular intensities. The corrected image \({I}^{{\prime} }(x,y)\) was computed as,.

For every soma and the designated ring configuration, we reported pre- and post-subtraction statistics within the inner measurement region (soma-adjacent ring):.

along with background noise estimates from the annulus:.

Recent findings suggest that along with \({\sigma }_{\text{STD}}\) (sample standard deviation). After the removal of local background, the above-defined inner ring shows an improved local signal-to-noise ratio, and mWmC puncta signals stand out more.

According to recent reports, third, to define an internal control region and identify mWmC-positive cells in each section, we implemented automated identification of the control region and quantification of mWmC+ cells. In this pipeline, we used an automated depth-aware sliding-window analysis. For each cell i, the locally background-corrected fluorescence intensity was summarized by the mean pixel intensity within the soma’s inner measurement ring after local background subtraction, as described above. Cell centroids were computed from the segmentation mask, and a sliding window of height 800 µm was moved along the pial-to-deep axis in 100-µm increments. Within each window w, we computed the cumulative fluorescence energy as \({S}_{w}=\sum _{i\in w}{I}_{i},\) where Ii is the per-cell fluorescence metric (post-subtraction inner ring mean intensity in this case). Windows with fewer than 15 cells were excluded. The resulting curve Sw versus depth was smoothed with a seven-point moving average, and the valley (minimum) among valid windows was selected as the centre of the control region, corresponding to the zone of lowest cumulative signal (background). From this valley, the control region was symmetrically expanded until at least 600 cells were included. The final control region was exported as a rectangular ROI spanning the full mediolateral width. For all cells within the control ROI, Ii were aggregated to estimate the control population mean (μctrl) and standard deviation (σctrl). We then defined mWmC+ cells using the below threshold: after trimming the top 2% of brightest cells to exclude outliers confounded by, for example, neighbouring overexposed pixels, thresholds for positive detection were defined as T5σ = μctrl + 5σctrl as the baseline to register mWmC+ cells.

Industry observers note that finally, with the per-cell mWmC information, we further assigned a cell type as mWmC+ (retino-recipient) by first deriving the mWmC+ cell profiles across different cell types using the methods described above. Encouragingly, automatically assigned mWmC+ cell profiles correlate strongly with manual annotations, indicating consistency across methods. To quantify enrichment of mWmC+ cells across neuronal subtypes, we computed an enrichment score for each tracing and cell type using the following steps. For each tracing × cell type, we constructed a 2 × 2 table of mWmC+ and mWmC− counts inside the cell type versus all other cells and applied a one-tailed Fisher’s exact test (alternative = “greater”). The odds ratio (OR) was computed as:.

According to recent reports, where a and b are the numbers of mWmC+ and mWmC− cells within the given subtype, and c and d are the corresponding counts outside that subtype. The effect size was visualized as log2(OR) (values < 0 clipped to 0). At the same time, statistical evidence was encoded by a point area proportional to −log10(P). Cell types with positive enrichment (log2(OR) > 0) were highlighted with a red outline (Fig. 2o). We assign a cell type as positive or connected under a specific tracing condition when the log2(OR) value is greater than 0 (enrichment). Based on the mWmC+ cell types assigned here, we summarized the mean mWmC+ cell proportion across animals (error bar: s.e.m.) as bar plots (Figs. 1k and 3c).

The neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. To determine parameters better reflect internal data structure and cell-type granularity, we chose clustering parameters based on statistical assessment and established parameter selection tools. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. The parameter selections here allowed us to settle on a granularity of cell types that best represent the internal data structure in an unbiased way. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below. Subsequent comparisons to published SC atlas showed high consistency, for example, when compared to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain Atlas at supertype level, supporting the robustness of selected parameters and the resulting granularity of cell types.

It has been revealed that to perform clustering and dimension reduction, we first applied SCTransform-based normalization67 to the expression matrix for each MERFISH section. This was enabled by accessing the SCTransform algorithm implemented in the R package via rpy2 from Python. Prior to normalization, raw counts were stored in adata.layers[‘raw_counts’]. A quality control filtering step was then applied to remove low-quality features, retaining genes detected in at least 5 cells (sc.pp.filter_genes) and cells with a total count of at least 5 (sc.pp.filter_cells). After filtering, the sparse matrices were explicitly sorted to ensure compatibility. Each AnnData object was converted to a Seurat object (as.Seurat()), and SCTransform was applied (do.correct.umi = FALSE). SCTransform models sequencing depth (library size/total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)) as a technical covariate during normalization. The full set of normalized gene expression values was extracted from the SCT assay’s scale.data slot and stored in adata.layers[‘normalized’], ensuring that any genes missing post-normalization were reintroduced as zero-filled vectors to retain consistency with the original feature set. The normalized matrix was then assigned to adata.X for downstream analysis. Raw counts were preserved in adata.raw, and standard quality control metrics (n_genes_by_counts, total_counts) were computed using the raw layer. Based on the quality control metrics, two sections with low quality and significantly lower counts were excluded from further analysis.

The AnnDatas of the remaining MERFISH slices were subsequently merged using scanpy (v1.10.4; abbreviated as sc onwards) with ad.concat (merge = ‘unique’, index_unique=None), yielding a combined dataset of 47,740 cells. Cell identifiers were made unique across slices, and principal component analysis was performed on the merged expression matrix (sc.tl.pca). The variance explained by each component was examined to guide dimensionality reduction (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). A neighbourhood graph was constructed using the top 15 principal components (n_pcs = 15) and 30 nearest neighbours (n_neighbors = 30) by sc.pp.neighbors. UMAP was then applied for two-dimensional embedding (sc.tl.umap). Unsupervised clustering was carried out using the Leiden algorithm with a resolution parameter of 0.8 (sc.tl.leiden). We examined the distribution of quality control metrics across the clusters. We found high consistency of n_genes_by_counts and total_counts across clusters except lower detection rate in one cluster (Extended Data Fig. 1h), which was identified as non-neuronal cells via the SC XGBoost classifier as described above (Extended Data Fig. 1i). To improve classification resolution, the non-neuronal cluster was excluded, yielding 46,277 high-quality transcriptomic profiles for neuronal cells. The neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below.

Industry observers note that to robustly identify the molecular identity of the above-identified MERFISH clusters, we took the following steps to classify the identified clusters and compare them to established SC atlases: first, we examined the gene expression pattern for a set of SC canonical marker genes (Fig. 1g) and the dendrogram between these clusters based on hierarchical clustering of averaged expression per cluster (sc.tl.dendrogram). Second, we aligned our MERFISH data to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain (CCN20230722) taxonomy30 using the MapMyCells tool suite from the Allen Institute. Third, we utilized the XGBoost classifier, as described above, to link the MERFISH data to our and other published SC scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq neuron-type atlases6,27,28, using the shared genes between the MERFISH panel and the snRNA-seq genes as features (Extended Data Fig. 2c,g,j). Finally, we compared the expression pattern of key marker genes between our data and previously published SC datasets (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, the identified clusters captured the neuronal diversity of the SC at high resolution, demonstrating strong concordance—and in some cases, enhanced granularity—compared to established reference atlases.

Recent findings suggest that we implemented a sublaminar-controlled cell-type specificity analysis to test the specificity of each SC type in specifying the connections with presynaptic RGC inputs (Fig. 2d). The analysis is based on a permutation-based statistical framework with Stouffer z-score aggregation across mice. More specifically, to assess cell-type–specific enrichment or depletion of mWmC+ labelling independent of sublaminar distribution, we performed a sublaminar-controlled permutation test. Within each mouse, SC neurons were binned by soma depth (50 µm unless otherwise specified). Within each (animal × depth bin) stratum, cell-type labels were randomly shuffled, thereby preserving the sublaminar distribution of mWmC labelling while disrupting the association between cell-type identity and mWmC labelling. All permutation tests were performed with 1,000 permutations using a fixed random seed unless otherwise stated. For each permutation, we computed the number of mWmC+ cells per cell type, yielding a null distribution of expected counts under the hypothesis that sublaminar position alone explains connectivity. Observed mWmC+ cell counts were then converted into per-animal z-scores relative to this null distribution. Specifically, for each cell type t and mouse q, the z-score was computed as follows,.

where \({N}_{t,q}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes the observed number of mWmC+ cells of type t in mouse q, and μt,q and σt,q denote the mean and standard deviation of the permutation-derived null distribution for that cell type and mouse. z-Scores provide a signed, normalized measure of enrichment or depletion relative to sublaminar expectation. z-Scores were then aggregated across mice using Stouffer’s method as below,.

where n is the number of mice. To test for bidirectional deviations (enrichment or depletion) of mWmC labelling beyond sublaminar expectation, two-sided P values were computed from the combined z-scores using the standard normal distribution as,.

Sources indicate that and controlled for multiple comparisons across cell types using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Positive z-scores indicate enrichment beyond sublaminar expectation, whereas negative z-scores indicate depletion, reflecting cases in which sublaminar position alone overestimates the likelihood of receiving retinal input. As statistical inference is performed using normal-theory P values derived from the aggregated z-scores (after estimating null mean and variance from permutations), the minimum attainable P value is not constrained by the number of permutations. Finally, SC neuron types were ranked by their aggregated Stouffer z-scores, which we refer to as the cell-type specificity score, representing the preference of a cell type’s molecular identity for RGC connectivity (Fig. 2e).

Sources indicate that RGC axons in the SC from four different genotypes and all RGCs were included. In brief, coronal brain sections were immunostained and imaged using a confocal microscope, as previously described43. Confocal stacks of 20 µm thickness were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Using ImageJ, each right SC hemisphere was divided into five equal sections. The fluorescence profile of axon arbors was measured by taking 200-μm-thick line scans perpendicular to each section’s pial surface, extending to a depth of 500 μm below it. Signal intensity values were normalized to the maximum intensity across images and plotted. The locally weighted scatterplot smoothing function in MATLAB was used to smooth the curve. ImageJ was used to analyse confocal stacks and produce maximum-intensity projections. To quantify axon depth across the SC, the shortest distance from the pial surface to the upper and lower boundaries of the axonal arbors was measured within each section. Five mice of each genotype, including all SC slices, were used for each experimental condition. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit/random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

The retina histology protocol was described as previously described50. Mice were euthanized, and eyes were collected, then fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 1 h on ice. Retinas were dissected and rinsed with PBS. For the whole-mount retina data in Fig. 3, we adapted previously described protocols37. Whole-mount retina samples were blocked in blocking buffer (5% normal donkey serum, 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS) at room temperature for 1 h, then incubated with primary antibodies for 2–4 days at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. For mounting, retinas were placed flat, ganglion cell side up, and sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For retinal vertical sections in Extended Data Fig. 6, we adapted protocols previously described37. Fixed mouse retinas were cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS for 1 h before embedding in OCT (Epredia). Vertical retinal cryosections (20 µm) were prepared and mounted on glass slides. Sections were blocked in the same blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

Recent findings suggest that brain section histology was described previously68. Mice were deeply anaesthetized and perfused transcardially with ice-cold PBS, followed by 4% PFA. Brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissue blocks sank. Tissue was frozen directly on the stage of a sliding microtome (Leica) cooled with dry ice and sectioned coronally at 40 µm. Free-floating sections were blocked in the blocking buffer described above and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, then for 1 h at room temperature with secondary antibodies. Sections were mounted on slides with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

In a recent development, we imaged calcium responses in mice using a two-photon microscope (Neurolabware) with a Spectra-Physics MaiTai laser at 920 nm (15–50 mW) to excite GCaMP6s. Imaging in the SC was performed at depths of 50–200 µm below the pia surface. A 575 × 370 µm field of view was scanned at 15.5 Hz, producing a series of 416 × 268-pixel images. A tangent LCD screen (Dell, U2312HM) placed in front of the left eye of head-fixed mice will present a visual stimulus generated with Psychtoolbox3 (MATLAB) and synchronized with image acquisition via TTL signals from the stimulus screen. The screen is centred 14 cm away from the mouse, angled at 20 degrees in pitch and yaw to minimize fisheye distortion. We imaged each mouse for about 1 h, with multiple sessions on successive days if needed to present a battery of visual stimuli and acquire stable imaging.

In a recent development, visual stimuli were presented on a tangent (1,920 × 1,080 pixels) region of the screen. The screen was strobed for 2 µs at the end of each scan line (1,200 Hz; luminance of the grey screen, 1.25 cd m−2; maximum brightness, 1/80 of the unmodified monitor) to minimize interference between the visual stimulus and two-photon fluorescence detection. All stimuli presented used only the green and blue channels of the screen. Red bars flickered periodically at the bottom of the screen, which was covered with black tape, to convey the timing of the visual stimulus to synchronize with fluorescence acquisition. All visual stimuli in two-photon experiments were presented in a pseudorandom sequence, interspersed with blank periods within each stimulus block, using a different random seed for each block. Moving gratings were used to test the direction selectivity of SC neurons. The drifting grating was 100 pixels wide (6.4°), with black or white bars, and drifted in 8 directions (45° intervals) at a speed of 356 pixels per second (22.7° per second). To map receptive fields, flashing spots were presented in a 9 × 5 position arrayed across the stimulus monitor. Each spot was a 216 × 216 pixel (13.8° × 13.8°) square that appeared for 1 second. All visual stimuli were repeated six times per trial.

In a recent development, to test the contribution of the ipsilateral eye to the direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons, we covered the ipsilateral eye with a black box during calcium imaging. The box was removed after the experiments.

According to recent reports, we performed offline motion correction of calcium imaging data by NoRMCorre73, identified GCaMP6s+ cells, extracted calcium traces for each cell, and subtracted neuropil signals. Next, we aligned traces to visual stimuli using synchronization pulses relayed from stimulus monitors to the microscope via a TTL signal, which were time-stamped in the imaging data. For traces with high-peak noisy spikes (large mouse motion that cannot be corrected), we used a denoising algorithm to replace noisy dots with smooth traces. The noisy spike traces were determined by whether any points were bigger than the mean ± 4 s.d. traces. Then, calcium traces were aligned to the onset of each visual stimulus, averaged across trials, and the peak and valley of each mean trace were identified.

DSI calculation followed a previously published protocol74. ΔF/F values for each presentation of a stimulus were averaged from six repeats, and the peak ΔF/F for each direction was used to compute direction preference. The direction selectivity index (DSI) was calculated as the normalized amplitude of the vector sum of all directions by their scalar sum. Cells with DSI > 0.2 were classified as direction selective. The preferred direction was defined as the weighted vector sum over eight stimulus angles.

To quantify immunostained cells in the SC and retina, confocal images of vertical retinal sections, coronal SC sections, and whole-mount retina were collected under identical imaging conditions across all samples. Confocal stacks of 20 µm (retina and SC sections) or 60 µm (whole-mount retina) were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Cells positive for each marker was identified using thresholded fluorescence intensity criteria. For RNAscope in situ hybridization, SC sections processed with RNAscope and immunostaining were imaged on a Zeiss LSM900 with a 20× objective. The number of GFP-positive neurons or marker-positive cells was counted across all stained samples as mentioned above. Data were pooled across animals, and results are presented as percentages (mean ± s.e.m.). Confocal image files for histology were analysed using Fiji Image J (v1.53c), Microsoft Excel 365, Graph Pad Prism9, Adobe Illustrator 2020. Electrophysiological data collection and analysis were not performed blindly with respect to the experimental conditions. All whole-cell recording data were acquired by Camplex 10.7 (Molecular Devices) and analysed in MATLAB (MathWorks) or Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices). Optogenetically evoked currents were averaged across 5 trials. Clampfit 10.7 measured the peak amplitudes of evoked currents. MATLAB analysed the intrinsic properties of recorded neurons. All statistics were calculated by GraphPad Prism 9. Peak currents between the two groups were compared using a two-tailed Student’s t-test.

In a recent development, optomotor response was described previously75. The OptoDrum (Striatech) comprises a box with four screens to simulate drifting gratings. An IR camera mounted on the top of the box was used to record mouse movements. Mice were first acclimated to the room in their cages for 30 min. Then, freely moving mice were placed on a platform and allowed to acclimate to the box for at least 5 min. Drifting gratings (12° s−1) in the clockwise direction can trigger left-eye-mediated body and head movements, while drifting gratings in the counterclockwise direction were used to test right-eye-mediated movements. Drifting gratings were presented from low spatial frequencies (0.056 cycles per degree) to high frequencies (0.3–0.5 cycles per degree) to determine the threshold at which a mouse could track. OptoDrum’s software can detect the body shape of mice and label the positions of head, body, and tail of mice. The stimulus and video tracking were paused if a mouse engaged in grooming behaviour or dropped off the platform and resumed later. The software can score the optomotor response and determine the spatial-frequency threshold. False positives were manually identified as invalid, and the same frequency of drifting gratings was repeated. We compared the spatial-frequency threshold of drifting gratings to trigger optomotor responses in the left eye (ablation) with the right eye (control) to assess visual acuity differences.

We obtained measurements from distinct biological samples. No covariates were tested. No formal test of normality was performed; statistical tests were selected based on the distributional assumptions of the data. Statistical methods and the number of animals tested for each configuration are documented in the figure legends for each experiment. When comparing two groups, statistics were derived using an unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test or Fisher’s exact test, as indicated in the figure legends. For comparing cell-type proportions across multiple reactions, we used the Kruskal–Wallis H test (scipy.stats.kruskal, Python). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed in GraphPad Prism 9 to assess the statistical significance of differences among multiple measurements.

Fisher’s exact test was performed using the Easy Fisher Exact Test Calculator (https://www.socscistatistics.com/tests/fisher/default2.aspx).

Industry observers note that statistical significance was defined as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001. All values indicate mean ± s.e.m., unless otherwise noted.

a, Unsupervised classification of sSC using the standard fresh-frozen MERFISH protocol. UMAP embedding of 5,845 cells reveals consistent clustering of the same 8 ENCs and 11 INCs identified with TransA-MERFISH on fixed tissue (Fig. 1d). Cell-type labels were assigned to Leiden clusters based on canonical marker gene expression patterns and transcriptomic mapping via a supervised XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH atlas. b, Confusion matrix showing transcriptomic correspondence between cell types in standard MERFISH (rows) and TransA-MERFISH (columns). c, Violin plots comparing quality control metrics between standard MERFISH (blue) and TransA-MERFISH (gray). Distributions are highly similar across key metrics, including the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts), total transcript counts per cell (total_counts), and cell mask area (in pixels). A modest reduction in n_genes_by_counts and total_counts was observed in TransA-MERFISH experiments. d, Comparison of matched neuronal subtype frequencies between standard MERFISH and TransA-MERFISH. Values are plotted on a ln-ln scale to highlight low-frequency types. A strong correlation is observed across both excitatory and inhibitory populations, indicating that the TransA-MERFISH protocol did not bias or deplete neuron types in the sSC (Pearson R = 0.88). e, Validation accuracies of the XGBoost classifier trained using various gene selection strategies: the performance of the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel was compared to randomly sampled 140-gene sets drawn from either the full single-cell transcriptome or the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs). Additional gene sets were constructed by selecting the top k specific genes (Methods) per SC neuronal cluster (k = 1–10), based on 19 neuronal clusters identified from re-clustering of the neuronal subset of the dataset28. Data are presented as mean ± SD. f, Dot plots comparing the expression patterns of 2 non-optimal probes (top row, blue) with their corresponding expressions in snRNA-seq17 (bottom row, orange). MERFISH cells are grouped according to their predicted snRNA-seq cluster identities, as inferred by Tangram-based imputation (Methods). The 140-gene list is presented in Supplementary Table 1. g-j, Classification and filtering of non-neuron cells (NNs). UMAP embedding (g) of all high-quality cells (47740 cells after quality filtering, see Methods) before filtering out non-neuronal cells, colored by broad cell classes: excitatory neurons (ENCs), inhibitory neurons (INCs), and NNs. NNs were identified using a supervised XGBoost classifier (i) trained on an SC snRNA-seq dataset, as in the reference28. Violin plots (h) of quality control metrics show that NNs exhibit reduced numbers of detected genes per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts per cell (total_counts), consistent with the design principles for neurons in the TransA-MERFISH gene panel. Bar plots (j) showing the average proportions of ENCs and INCs among all detected cells across animals. NNs were subsequently filtered out before re-clustering of neuronal cells to improve classification resolution among neuronal types. n = 16 animals. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

a,b, Transcriptomic correspondence between the MERFISH-based sSC neuron atlas and the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (CCN20230722; Allen Institute)20. (a) UMAP embedding of the TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), colored by the most probable mapped supertype identity inferred via MapMyCells. (b) Confusion matrix showing the correspondence between TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (rows) and 10 x WMB supertypes (columns), as determined by MapMyCells mapping (Methods). c, Transcriptomic correspondence between the TransA-MERFISH sSC neuron atlas and the Trans-Seq single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) SC neuron atlas9, as determined by XGBoost-based classification (Methods). Your weekly briefing on Chelsea, featuring team news and expert analysis from Dom Smith.

It has been revealed that I would like to be emailed about offers, event and updates from Evening Standard. Read our privacy notice.

Xabi Alonso has delivered an patch on Joao Pedro’s fitness as Chelsea prepare to host Leeds in the Premier League on Saturday.

The Brazilian striker was a shock absentee from the team-sheet as the Blues welcomed arch-rivals Tottenham to Stamford Bridge last month, with Alonso later revealing he had suffered a thigh injury in training.

That saw him ruled out from the Tottenham match through to the November international break, after which it was hoped he would be fit to return.

But Alonso has now confirmed that there has been no such luck, and that Joao Pedro will play no part in the match against Leeds on Saturday.

Speaking at his pre-match press conference on Friday, the Spaniard confirmed he had yet to even return to training, suggesting he will not be returning to the pitch any time soon.

“Not yet,” the Spaniard replied when asked about his No9. “He’s not ready to train yet for the team. Not for Leeds no. We need to see day by day how he is feeling.”.

There are concerns behind the scenes at Chelsea he could remain sidelined until the new year.

That is, of course, bad news for the Blues, who have been generally off the boil without Joao Pedro as an attacking focal point. Of the four matches since his injury, the Blues have won only once, against crisis-stricken Manchester United.

That result came amid a run of three defeats by Tottenham, Sunderland, and Liverpool, who required a penalty shootout to knock Chelsea out of the Carabao Cup.

With Joao Pedro sidelined, here is how our Chelsea correspondent Dom Smith thinks the Blues will line up against Leeds...

Chelsea predicted XI vs Leeds (3-4-2-1): Martinez; Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill; Neto, Caicedo, Lavia, Chavarria; Estevao, Palmer; Rogers.

Injured: Joao Pedro, James, Lacroix, Hato.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada has insisted he was not involved ‘in any wrongdoings’ during his time at Manchester City amid the ongoing case against his former employers.

An independent commission found City guilty of breaching more than 100 of the Premier League’s financial rules in September between the period of 2009 and 2018.

City have appealed against the ruling and repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.

Berrada joined United in January 2024 having spent over a decade working in various roles for City Football Group.

He was named the club’s CEO in 2016 and remained in that role until 2020 when he was named City Football Group’s chief football operations officer for the next four years.

Industry observers note that berrada’s time at the club’s CEO overlaps with the period in which City were investigated. But the United chief has no concerns over any implications for him in the case.

‘I’m not concerned,’ Berrada told Sky Sports.

‘I want to be very clear about this: I wasn’t involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn’t involved in the proceedings. There are no allegations against me.

‘In that sense, there will be no surprises.’.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Asked whether United could look to pursue compensation if City fail in their appeal, Berrada replied: ‘I don’t want to comment on that because right now, it’s an ongoing process.

‘When it runs its course, then we’ll take a view on what is our position as Manchester United.’.

Berrada and the rest of United’s hierarchy have just presided over their third mid-season managerial sacking in three years with Mauricio Pochettino the latest to be tasked with lifting the club from its malaise.

‘If you think about the fact that we’ve had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven’t achieved the stability that we want to – that’s for sure,’ Berrada remarked.

Sources indicate that ‘There are different circumstances as to why it didn’t work out with Erik, Ruben and now Michael. And we’re always learning. We’re always trying to improve and understand what has failed.’.

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

The three significant guns of his attack were primed and ready to come on in the next break in play when Arsenal at last broke through in this, their second Champions League league phase game of the season against some stubborn opposition from Ligue 1. Lille had sat deep against an Arsenal attack without Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, and the French club were past the hour when it all finally broke.

Industry observers note that that was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. They had created some chances and at times looked promising, but as soon as the massive three were on the difference was obvious.

Sources indicate that this touch and finish from Jurriën Timber 😮‍💨 Arsenal lead against Lille! 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/L2B6YsNDXo.

“We had moments in the game in the first half … [when] we arrived in very dangerous positions,” Arteta mentioned. “With a lot of advantage, our technical quality wasn’t good enough to deliver moments of real threat and especially to be able to sustain the attack, so we allowed certain transitions.” He said that he made some changes at half-time, as managers are wont to do, and that things improved but the real change was clear when he made the substitutions.

“It was a joy to watch,” Arteta mentioned. “The three goals were unbelievable, the connections, the timings, the quality they delivered to score. Three different players and a lot of players participating in those goals, so overall very, very happy.” He had played Myles Lewis-Skelly at left-back again to give Riccardo Calafiori a rest. Saka had been ill during the week and not in a position to start.

Industry observers note that in the opposing technical area was Davide Ancelotti, the 37-year-old son of Carlo, with his father’s trademark slow amble to the edge of the technical area. Young Ancelotti had drilled his team well, but once they were exposed to the high-pace recovery and sharp passing geometry of the Arsenal substitutes there was to be no coming back. Saka made the second for Eberechi Eze who had started the game on the left and the Arsenal No 7 scored the third himself. The home fans sang again about being champions of England and they certainly looked the part.

It didn't take Arsenal long to double their lead ⚡️ Eberechi Eze scores to make it 2-0 🎯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/BVMieESgbi.

According to recent reports, it took a while. Arteta got ever more sour in his dealings with Richard Hempel, the giant German fourth official. Industry observers note that arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

Sources indicate that as Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”.

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Recent findings suggest that lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

According to recent reports, leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

AC Milan have had a long-standing interest in Tiago Gabriel and they may now have found an open door for the mercato.

There have been plenty of links between Milan and defenders in recent weeks and months. Of course, a few names are repeated in this time and Goncalo Inacio is the one that most Milanisti will be familiar with.

According to recent reports, however, Gabriel’s is another. Since even before the summer, the Portuguese defender has been linked with a move to San Siro and it could well come true in the next mercato if things don’t align with other targets.

In fact, Tuttomercatoweb (via MilanNews) now reports that, thanks to help from Jorge Mendes, the club could sign him in the upcoming mercato. Similarly to Mario Gila, he’d be valued at around €30 million, but that price could be negotiated, of course.

“There was some discussion on the last day of the [summer] transfer window, but when it comes to deals as significant and important as that of Tiago Gabriel, there isn’t even enough time to set up negotiations on the last day of the transfer window.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United’s CEO Omar Berrada has hit back at criticism of the club’s transfer strategy last summer and insists a ‘disciplined’ approach is required.

United spent £155 million on signing three midfielders in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba in the summer transfer window.

However, Mauricio Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford this week without a recognised striker as Benjamin Sesko is out for the remainder of the year with a shin problem, while Luke Shaw has missed United’s last seven games due to injury.

United supporters have criticised the club’s decision to only strengthen Michael Carrick’s midfield in the summer but Berrada is adamant the squad is ‘fundamentally better’ after their signings.

‘You have to take it in the context of the last few years,’ Berrada told Sky Sports.

‘The summer of 2025, I think the recruitment team was widely praised with the four players that were signed. And they did very well. They helped the team achieve Champions League qualification.

Industry observers note that ‘When we look at this summer, we went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play. It’s probably been the summer or the transfer window where there’s been the highest inflation in transfer fees.

Industry observers note that ‘And we’ve stated publicly and we’ve said consistently in the last few years that we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players for the right value at the right time in terms of what the squad needs.

‘And when we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we’re receiving a lot of criticism for it but we’re actually happy with the players that we bought.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow, and let’s not forget that we’ve also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona – these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

In a recent development, ‘It’s true that we lost Casemiro, who is a top player and gave a lot to the club. We also lost Manuel Ugarte to, unfortunately, an ACL injury. So our focus was very much about straightening the midfield.

‘When we started the transfer window, we really only had Kobbie Mainoo as our midfielder. So we wanted to reinforce that, and we did it.’.

Berrada also addressed United’s decision not to sign a new left-sided defender after the club made an enquiry for Newcastle United’s Lewis Hall in the summer.

‘When you look at the other areas of the pitch, and there’s a lot of discussion about the back line,’ Berrada said.

Industry observers note that ‘But we did come into it thinking we have depth. We have nine players that can play in the back line, in the back four positions.

‘So that’s why we looked primarily at investing in the midfield. But we were always looking for opportunities. I think it’s been widely reported that we were looking at potentially the left-back position as a reinforcement.

It has been revealed that ‘I think what we’ve seen in the back line is we’ve had injuries, it’s taken Matthijs de Ligt longer than we would want it to get back. Unfortunately, Luke Shaw suffered a muscle injury that meant he was out for five or six weeks.

In a recent development, ‘So could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players and you have to find the right players at the right value.

‘There’s no point in us spending £40 million, £50m for players that we’re not convinced are going to add value to the team.

‘So it’s always about being disciplined and finding the right opportunities and getting the right players that are going to take us forward.

‘When I talk about being disciplined, I talk about not overspending on players that don’t necessarily add quality to the team.

‘Because when you sign a player that doesn’t work out for Man Utd, it becomes very difficult to move that player on or to get the sale we want. And that can set us back.

Industry observers note that ‘So when I talk about being disciplined, I’m not talking about necessarily not spending to get the top players. We have the ambition to win, to win the Premier League, to win the Champions League, to win the domestic cups. And for that, we need top talent. So when we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don’t want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it.’.

Niko Kovac insisted Ethan Nwaneri will "play many more games" for Borussia Dortmund, but faces "fierce competition" for minutes.

Nwaneri joined BVB on loan in the summer from Arsenal, but has struggled to make his mark for the Bundesliga side in 2026-27.

The 19-year-old has made 12 appearances for Dortmund this season, with four of those coming as a starter, but is yet to record a direct goal contribution.

However, the teenager impressed for England's Under-21s during the international break, assisting twice in a win over France's Under-21s.

Kovac was impressed with Nwaneri's performances during the break, and has backed the Arsenal loanee to make an impact ahead of their trip to Borussia Monchengladbach on Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that "We're delighted about that. It was a friendly in which he did really well. And that's why we signed him," Kovac remarked when asked about Nwaneri's display against France's U21s.

Industry observers note that "We have some very good players in those attacking positions. Kosta [Karetsas] has also returned now. The competition is fierce.

"He [Nwaneri] has played a lot of games and, at just 19 years of age, he will certainly play many more games for us.".

We are B V B. https://t.co/SdauOUTZZz.
